title: How do you get commercial-level game aesthetics with Codex?
author: MarcoSalernoDevelop
selftext:
Hi guys, I've been a programmer for more than 20 years. I started when I was a child and always wanted to make my own videogames.

I was always held back by having zero skills or patience for graphics, modeling, and so on, but I have a strong technical background and a lot of ideas.

I wanted to try making my cool games with AI. I have a Codex Plus subscription and wanted to give it a try, so I set up an environment with Codex, Astra on High mode, Blender, and Godot.

My aim was to be just the art director and let AI do most of the hard work.

Unfortunately, I've only managed to get very low-quality assets, even after having ChatGPT create the prompts, MD files, and project setup for me.

What am I doing wrong? I see a lot of beautiful results from people using the same setup.

Can someone explain how you're achieving such good results? I see a lot of you saying you're not even using any base assets, but idk, it feels like my Astra is much more stupid (and yes, my prompts probably are too, but still...).

PS: I know the Plus subscription doesn't let me do super-long runs. I just wanted to start testing things by making small parts one by one, staying within the given usage limits.

replies.author: daddywookie

This is the most important thing. Can you describe why an asset isn't good? Can you compare two assets and say why one is better than the other? Can you clearly define what you are trying to achieve, both in writing and with examples.

Just like anything AI, the more you know and the more you can feed into the context the better the results you can get.

comments.author: SeasawPhilosopher
comments.body:
Similar journey to you, coding 30 years, 20 years as a software engineer, and went all in on AI game dev 5 weeks ago. The art has been very frustrating, but I’m getting better day over day, it’s about learning to be an art director. I had pretty good taste before but I could only tell stuff that looked good vs bad and had no idea how to direct art. Have codex or Claude’s teach you the fundamentals of environment and character art and just integrate a new thing or two each day. Pretty soon you’ll hit and inflation point and start seeing your environments and being able to describe what they lack.

I knew nothing and now I’m directing environmental art by having it build up layered  textures, applying wear and environmental effects, and improving lighting and my scenes are actually starting to look good. For modeling I had Claude build me a system for rapidly generating concept art, iterating on concepts, cutting out asset images and constructing with meshy.

Things that were big unlocks   
Concept art  
Reference images   
Grey box paint overs  
Substance designer and painter, Claude and codex use it really well  
Having chat got teach me the fundamentals of texturing, lightening, effects, rendering etc

replies.author: startyourengines
replies.body: I'll also add that adding "passes" to your AI-driven art pipeline can do wonders. Using simple skeletal/anatomical representations or (heavily simplified) CAD-like rules for objects / architecture can really push past slop. In general, I've had a lot more success with getting AI to write procedural passes than reliably hallucinate something AD-coherent, internally consistent, visually compelling, etc.

comments.author: notlemars
comments.body:
Ai art creation is proving to be the actual skill test and dividing line for this new era of game dev. We simply have to iterate and iterate, try new approaches, use new references, keep beating at it until it feels right and use that one small “right” as the source of all other art. 

What I tell myself is that “hey this is still faster than if I was a real artist.” 

On the bright side, with enough iteration, we shall step into differentiation.

comments.author: aura-32
comments.body: Most of the nice-looking stuff you see isn't from the model being smarter. It comes from a tight style constraint: a small fixed palette, one lighting setup and one texture approach, applied to everything. Pick a reference game, write down 5 to 10 concrete visual rules, and make every asset prompt follow them. Then spend your effort on lighting and post-processing in Godot. That's where low-poly stuff goes from "placeholder" to "stylised."
